paras: The attempted lynching of Stoney Ball took place at Belen, Valencia County, New Mexico Territory, on January 27, 1903, when a crowd seized Ball, a Black man from Albuquerque accused of assaulting a girl, and began hanging him from a telegraph pole before Sheriff Baca and a posse arrived by special train and took him away. Ball had been shot and beaten during his capture, and the Santa Fe New Mexican later reported that he died of those injuries in the Los Lunas jail. New Mexico papers in English and Spanish presented the accusation against Ball as fact.

According to the Las Vegas Daily Optic and the Spanish-language La Voz del Pueblo, Ball was an Albuquerque man who said he had worked at the White Elephant saloon. He was accused of attacking the fourteen-year-old daughter of P. Baca, "a highly respected citizen of Belen," as she walked to school in the morning; other reports called her "a little Mexican girl."

According to a Belen dispatch printed in La Voz del Pueblo, a force of men was organized at once and found Ball hiding on the bank of the Rio Grande. When he tried to defend himself the men fired on him, and a bullet through the thigh forced him to surrender; he was then brought before the girl, who identified him. The New Mexican later said he had also been "badly beaten about the head and face."

An Albuquerque special printed in the Arizona Republican said "a mob of Mexicans" had captured Ball and was "in the act of swinging him to a telegraph pole" when Sheriff Baca and a posse reached Belen on a special train "just in time." The sheriff took Ball to the county jail at Los Lunas, and La Voz del Pueblo wrote that he had to work hard to keep the people from lynching him.

A week later the Optic reported that Ball was very ill from "such severe handling from the mob at Belen" and might not recover. The girl's uncle, Eugenio Baca, said in the same item that Ball "failed to accomplish his purpose," though the girl was badly beaten. On February 7 the Albuquerque Weekly Citizen called that report "false," saying Ball was "getting along nicely" in the Los Lunas jail and would await the Valencia County grand jury.

Six days later the Santa Fe New Mexican reported that Ball had died in the jail "on Tuesday last," February 10, despite medical attention. It added that his wife in Albuquerque refused to have anything to do with his remains and that he was buried at Los Lunas on February 12. No report of an inquest, an arrest of anyone in the crowd, or grand jury action appears in the coverage.

Outside the territory the rescue ran as a two-sentence wire item, "Negro Rescued From a Mob" in the San Antonio Daily Light on January 28 and among the Americus Times-Recorder's "Flashes from the Wires" in Georgia the next day. The Arizona Republican headed its Denver special "A Negro Saved," crediting the sheriff while stating as fact that Ball "had critically assaulted a little girl."

New Mexico papers likewise treated the accusation as established: the Optic's exchange column said Ball "brutally assaulted and ravished" the girl, and La Voz del Pueblo headed its Belen dispatch "Un Negro Brutal," calling him "el bruto" and the would-be lynchers simply "el pueblo," the people. The Albuquerque Weekly Citizen took a mocking tone, saying Ball had "caused a whole lot of excitement at Belen" and would be fit "to wear the stripes" if convicted for "his Belen fun." The New Mexican ran his death as a brief city item, calling it "inevitable"; no Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The Citizen's denial that Ball was dying came three days before the date the New Mexican gave for his death, so the two reports are not strictly contradictory, but the New Mexican's is the only report of the death. Accounts of the captors also varied: the Arizona Republican described them as "a mob of Mexicans," while the Belen dispatch spoke of a force of men organized in the town.

accounts.label: Santa Fe New Mexican
accounts.gist: Ball died in the Los Lunas jail of his injuries and a gunshot wound on Tuesday, Feb 10, and was buried there after his wife refused his remains.

framing.detail: Two-sentence wire, 'Negro Rescued From a Mob', carried in Texas and in Georgia's 'Flashes from the Wires'.
Arizona Republican headline 'A Negro Saved' credits the sheriff's rescue while stating as fact that Ball 'had critically assaulted a little girl'.

La Voz del Pueblo headed its dispatch 'Un Negro Brutal', called Ball 'el bruto' and 'brutal malhechor', and treated the accusation as proven; the Optic likewise said he 'brutally assaulted and ravished' the girl.
The Albuquerque Weekly Citizen mocked Ball, saying he had 'caused a whole lot of excitement at Belen' and would 'wear the stripes' for 'his Belen fun'.
Santa Fe New Mexican ran the death as a brief city item, repeating the accusation as fact and calling his death 'inevitable'.
